issues.legal_issue: Statutory finality of an assessment order does not by itself bar constitutional writ review where the levy is illegal.
material_facts: The assessments taxed income from fruits and fallen trees that had been held to be agricultural income and outside the income tax imposed under the relevant law.
The assessments for the later years had become final because the taxpayer did not pursue the available statutory remedies for those years.
The taxpayer sought writ relief after the assessments had become final.
issues.conclusion: Statutory finality does not, by itself, prevent a court from exercising writ jurisdiction to review an illegal levy, although the Court did not decide whether the assessments were nullities or whether a refund was thereby due.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226 of the Constitution, constitutional review is not excluded merely because an assessment has attained statutory finality if the levy is illegal. The Court distinguished Commissioner of Income Tax v. Tribune Trust, where the assessment was within the officer’s jurisdiction and the disputed claim concerned a statutory exemption; it did not decide whether the assessments here were nullities.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A taxpayer seeks constitutional writ review of a tax assessment.
predicates.levy_is_illegal: The tax was imposed on income that was not legally taxable by the assessing authority.

issues.definition: If a taxpayer seeks constitutional writ review of a tax assessment and the levy was illegal, assessment finality alone does not bar writ review.

issues.legal_issue: A prolonged and inadequately explained delay may justify refusal of writ relief, and the Supreme Court will not disturb the High Court’s discretionary refusal absent an arbitrary or improper exercise of discretion.
material_facts: The taxpayer waited years after the assessments and several years after the favorable ruling on the character of the income before filing the writ petition.
The taxpayer attributed the delay to an expectation that the tax authorities would adjust the other assessments automatically, which the Court regarded as illusory.
The High Court refused relief on the ground of laches, and the Supreme Court found that it had not exercised its discretion arbitrarily or improperly.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s refusal of writ relief on the ground of laches was upheld, and the Supreme Court declined to disturb that discretionary decision.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 relief is subject to temporal and discretionary restraints, and a court may ordinarily deny relief for unexplained and undue delay. The Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court’s discretionary refusal unless its exercise is arbitrary, improper, or otherwise untenable.

rule.if: appeal_from_writ_denial and prolonged_unexplained_delay and high_court_refused_relief_for_laches and high_court_discretion_not_arbitrary

predicates.appeal_from_writ_denial: A party appeals to the Supreme Court after a High Court refuses writ relief.
predicates.prolonged_unexplained_delay: The claimant waited an undue period to seek relief and did not provide an adequate explanation for the delay.
predicates.high_court_refused_relief_for_laches: The High Court denied relief because of the claimant’s delay.
predicates.high_court_discretion_not_arbitrary: The High Court’s exercise of discretion was not arbitrary or improper.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows a writ denial based on prolonged unexplained delay and the High Court’s discretion was not arbitrary, the Supreme Court declines to disturb that denial.

issues.legal_issue: A tax authority is not subject to mandamus to refund tax when no statutory duty requires it to do so, although the State may make an equitable refund voluntarily.
material_facts: The taxpayer asked the Central Board to direct refunds of tax paid under assessments that had become final.
The Court found no statutory duty requiring the Board to consider or grant the refund applications and doubted that the Board could exercise judicial power to direct refunds.
The Court stated that the State could nevertheless reconsider an illegally imposed tax and direct a refund, wholly or partly, on equitable grounds.
issues.conclusion: Mandamus could not issue to compel the Board to grant a refund because it had no statutory duty to do so; the State remained free to grant an equitable refund voluntarily.
issues.legal_principle: A writ of mandamus requires a statutory duty on the authority against which it is sought. Article 226 did not authorize compelling the Board to grant a refund where no such duty existed, though the State could act equitably on its own initiative.

predicates.refund_mandamus_proceeding: A claimant seeks a writ compelling a public authority to order a tax refund.
predicates.authority_has_no_statutory_refund_duty: No law requires the authority to consider or grant the requested refund.

issues.definition: If a claimant seeks to compel a public authority to order a refund and that authority has no statutory refund duty, mandamus to compel the refund is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate authority considering condonation of delay in a statutory tax appeal must consider intervening events without treating observations about delay in a writ proceeding as prejudicial to the taxpayer.
material_facts: The High Court had suggested that the taxpayer could file statutory appeals and seek condonation of delay.

The taxpayer’s proposed appeals concerned assessments made years earlier, during which the related dispute had proceeded through litigation and a favorable ruling on the character of the income had been given.

The Supreme Court endorsed the expectation that the appellate authority would give due regard to intervening events and stated that observations about delay in the writ proceeding must not prejudice the taxpayer’s condonation request.
issues.conclusion: If the taxpayer sought condonation of delay in statutory appeals, the appellate authority was to give due regard to intervening events, and the courts’ observations about delay in the writ proceeding were not to prejudice that decision.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 30(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, the appellate authority considering condonation of delay must give due regard to relevant intervening events; observations concerning delay in a separate writ proceeding are not to be used to the taxpayer’s prejudice in that consideration.

predicates.statutory_tax_appeal_seeking_delay_condo: A taxpayer seeks condonation of delay in filing a statutory tax appeal.
predicates.relevant_events_occurred_during_delay: Relevant litigation or other circumstances occurred during the period of delay.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer seeks condonation of delay in a statutory tax appeal and relevant events occurred during the delay, the appellate authority considers those events without treating writ-delay observations as prejudicial.
